machine.coverage_caveat: Single node type and effectively a single node for the topology results. No node-to-node variability study. Whether these NUMA tiers hold machine-wide is open.
machine.tool_validation: ptrchase, loaded_lat and bwmatrix were validated against Intel MLC on corsys4 (Xeon Gold 6246R) before use here: peak bandwidth within 0.6%, saturated latency within the random-vs-sequential delta.

declared_payload.captured: 2026-08-10 on frontier00126, inside an allocation, hwloc 2.11.2
declared_payload.note: --disallowed is required: without it lstopo exports only ALLOWED objects, the OS-reserved cores vanish from the file, and the declared payload silently agrees with our measurement. This export has 128 PUs / 64 Cores; the plain one had 112 / 56.

gpu_latency.note: ~8% run-to-run. Adequate for coarse tiers, NOT for distinguishing individual GCDs.

declared.levels: L1 32 KB, L2 512 KB, L3 32 MB per L3 region. The node has EIGHT L3 regions of 8 cores each (confirmed: 8 L3Cache objects in the hwloc XML); the four NPS4 NUMA domains each span two of them.

results.margin: Every plateau boundary lands on the declared size. Curves were taken one per NUMA DOMAIN (four), not one per L3 region (eight) -- the four sampled curves agree, but the eight L3 regions were not sampled independently.
results.note: Doubles as the calibration check for ptrchase on this machine. CORRECTION 2026-08-10: this entry previously read 'identical across all four CCDs', conflating the four NUMA domains with the CCD count. There are eight L3 regions. Caught by the treatment arm of the eval, which noticed the entry contradicted the eight OS-reserved cores (one per L3 region) recorded under cpu.core_inventory -- an internal inconsistency in the artifact, found by a consumer reading it.

declared.hwloc_implication: 56 usable cores of 64 present. hwloc reports the reservation correctly.
declared.note: Measured on frontier00126 2026-08-10 via hwloc 2.11.2. The declared sources DISAGREE WITH EACH OTHER: hwloc is right and the diagram is wrong. A user who runs lstopo gets the correct answer; a user who reads the node diagram does not.

results.margin: One core per L3 group is OS-reserved. `srun -c 56` is the ceiling; anything higher is rejected outright.
results.note: Verdict stays `misleading` but the target moves: it is the vendor diagram that misleads, not hwloc. Confirmed 2026-08-10 -- hwloc-calc reports 112 allowed of 128 topology PUs, reserved logical indices 112-127. This resolves the open question recorded in July.

results.margin: Loaded latency, peak bandwidth and cache hierarchy are equivalent on all four domains. The domains are genuine peers; only the crossing cost differs.
results.note: This confirmation is load-bearing for numa.distance_matrix: it establishes that the tier structure found there is a crossing cost, not domains being intrinsically different.

declared.source: ACPI SLIT via numactl -H, relayed by hwloc_distances_get
declared.implication: All four domains mutually equidistant; every remote hop costs 1.2x local.

results.margin: Near-to-far gap is 12.1 ns against a 1.2 ns noise floor (~10x), and 1353 MB/s against 289 MB/s (~4.7x). Two independently written tools -- one pointer-chasing, one streaming -- produce identical rank ordering across all six pairs, with perfect anti-correlation between latency and bandwidth.
results.consequence: Anything reading numa_distance() treats these four domains as interchangeable. Page placement and migration policy driven by the declared matrix systematically underestimates crossing cost.
results.note: Magnitudes differ 4x between metrics: latency spans 11% across pairs (18% counting local), bandwidth only 3.5% (4.9%). A bandwidth-only study would reasonably call these domains interchangeable. Which metric you measure determines whether you see the topology at all.
results.conditions_caveat: Measured on 4K pages because huge pages cannot be allocated on a remote domain here (see mem.page_backing). Absolute values run ~16 ns high; the local-vs-remote structure is unaffected.

declared.implication: One scalar per pair; direction not representable.

results.margin: 3.9 ns latency difference against a 1.2 ns floor (3.3x); 601 MB/s against 289 MB/s (2.1x). Both metrics agree on the direction -- 3->2 is better in both.
results.consequence: No scalar distance can express this. The declared model is not merely miscalibrated, it is structurally insufficient.
results.note: Confidence held at medium rather than high: the bandwidth margin is only 2.1x the floor. Worth a dedicated directional run before leaning on it in print.

measured.note: Each MI250X exposes two Graphics Compute Dies; the GCD is the unit ROCm and Slurm schedule.

results.margin: Factor of 2 between the package count on the diagram and the addressable device count.
results.consequence: A rank-per-GPU launch built from the diagram idles half the accelerator. Observed directly: the 1-rank QMCPACK run was starved twice over -- one OpenMP thread and one of eight GCDs.

corroboration.note: Both list eight devices, GPU[0]..GPU[7] / card0..card7, and agree on the mapping.

measured.probe: gpu_ptrchase --hostmatrix, host memory bound per NUMA domain and verified with move_pages
measured.outcome: No GCD row separates the domains by more than run-to-run noise. Across-pass spread 29-155 ns vs across-domain range 27-175 ns.
measured.rule: A row votes only when across-domain range exceeds 3x its worst across-pass spread. 0 of 8 rows cleared it.

results.margin: 0 of 8 rows can discriminate. Latency cannot resolve host-domain affinity on this machine with this probe.
results.consequence: This is the claim --gpu-bind=closest depends on, and it is currently taken on faith from the same vendor whose CPU distance table is contradicted above.
results.next_step: Not a probe-design failure so much as an effect-size problem: if the affinity penalty exists it is smaller than 8% run-to-run GPU latency variance. More passes would shrink the error bars; a larger buffer or a bandwidth-under-load probe might raise the signal.
results.note: The declared map is non-naive -- NUMA 0 pairs with GCD 4,5, not 0,1 -- which is precisely why it should not be assumed correct without measurement.

aggregate_observation.statement: Node 0 is the fastest host domain in 22 of 24 (GCD x pass) cells; chance is ~6. Column means 1250.6 / 1311.0 / 1331.7 / 1318.9 ns, a 60.5 ns margin.
aggregate_observation.why_not_a_claim: Uniform across GCDs. A real affinity effect would vary BY GCD and this does not. Leading explanation is our own probe: the task builds and memcpy's the 512 MiB chain on its main thread, unconfined under -c 56 and most likely resident on node 0.
aggregate_observation.discriminator: Re-run pinned to a different domain. If 'fastest' follows the thread it is our artifact; if it stays node 0 it is a machine property and deserves its own claim.

results.margin: No overlap between bands -- 79 ns of clear air between class 1 and 2, 139 ns between 2 and 3. Spacing is linear at ~10.8 ns per weight unit.
results.note: THE CONTROL. Same machine, same vendor, same firmware, two topology cost tables: the GPU weight table is accurate and linear, the CPU SLIT is flat and wrong. That turns numa.distance_matrix from 'firmware tables are unreliable' into 'AMD describes its GPU interconnect accurately and its CPU interconnect not at all' -- specific and actionable rather than lazy.

results.margin: L1 and L2 boundaries match the MI250X specification.
results.note: No stock tool reports pointer-chase latency on MI250X memory. This is a measurement gap gpu_ptrchase fills, not a re-measurement.

declared.source: THP sysfs + hugetlb pool + madvise return
declared.implication: A large-page request appears to succeed.

measured.outcome: Both normal paths to huge pages fail SILENTLY. Allocation succeeds; backing is 4K.

results.margin: Verified via smaps rather than trusting the madvise return.
results.consequence: Every latency measurement taken without verification is silently wrong and still looks plausible. Three experiments in this campaign produced clean, plausible, WRONG nulls for exactly this reason.
results.working_path: craype-hugepages2M is required, and it works by RELINKING the binary, not via a runtime flag.
results.secondary_defect: craype-hugepages2M provisions only the LOCAL node's pool. Once linked, the default allocator ABORTS under a remote `numactl -m`. Consequence for this campaign: local latency must be measured with the module and the NUMA matrix without it -- two separate passes, which is why numa.distance_matrix is on 4K pages.

conditions.note: -c 14 confines each rank to one NUMA domain; Cray MPICH refuses NIC_POLICY=NUMA otherwise. Placement verified per rank.

results.margin: Scaling is linear to 4 pairs: 22.7 -> 45.1 -> 90.3 GB/s. The node reaches 90.3 GB/s, ~90% of the declared 100 GB/s. The July 23.9 GB/s was PER LINK and the spec is correct; only the natural single-pair benchmark misleads.
results.consequence: Quoting the single-pair result next to the 100 GB/s node spec looks like a 4x error. The declared number is correct; the natural benchmark configuration measures something else.

control.question: Does MPICH_OFI_NIC_POLICY=NUMA do the work, or does rank spread?
control.finding: The policy does essentially NOTHING. What matters is spreading ranks across NUMA domains; the default policy then assigns NICs correctly on its own. Without this arm we would have credited the policy for a 4x speedup it had no part in -- and put that in the briefing as advice.

regimes.reason: PEAK. Working set still fits in L3 (32 MB per L3 region) but needs 8192 PTEs at 4K, far past TLB reach. Every access pays a page walk that itself goes to memory.
Both effects saturated; settles to a roughly constant offset

results.margin: Zero, then 2.4x, then a constant offset. There is no single number that describes this.
results.consequence: TLB misses reported as memory latency. The worst case is at a working set that still fits in cache, which is exactly where a developer would not look for it.
results.note: Latency effect only. Streaming bandwidth barely notices page size -- 107,765 huge vs 107,342 4K on corsys4 -- because sequential reads amortise the walk across a whole page.

results.margin: 98.3% of peak bandwidth is available at 2.7x lower latency. Between injection delay 52 and 56 latency collapses 634 -> 234 ns while bandwidth falls only 1.7%.
results.consequence: Tuning to saturate bandwidth costs a factor of 2.7 in latency for 1.7% of throughput.
results.cross_validation: Idle floor 89.0 ns agrees with ptrchase huge-page local (85.9 ns) and the cache curve DRAM plateau (87.9 ns) -- three measurements, two independent tools, within 3.5%.
results.method_note: The original 19-point sweep placed both knee endpoints inside a single gap and rendered the entire transition as one vertical jump. Densifying across 48-96 is what made the operating point visible.
results.open: A 400 ns step remains between delay 52 and 56. The transition is genuinely sharp but has not been proven with points inside it.
results.not_measured: Read/write mix. This probe sweeps read-only traffic; MLC sweeps ratios. Write traffic saturates differently.

results.margin: The 4 MiB bandwidth gap is 82x the across-pass spread; the latency gap is 30x. Device latency varied 0.02 us across three passes (0.011%) -- the most reproducible measurement in the campaign. Passes were INTERLEAVED, not blocked, so drift over the allocation cannot masquerade as a residency effect.
results.control: GPU-aware MPI run with HOST buffers on both ends landed within 0.02% of plain host. Enabling GPU support costs nothing by itself; the entire 5.5% lives in the hardware path between the NIC and the memory it reads. One run eliminated a whole hypothesis family.

eliminated.how: advantage is FLAT at 5.5% from 64 to 1024 pages, a 16x range. A scatter-gather cost would grow with page count. Nine independent points say it does not.

results.open: Contention versus cache coherence on host DMA. The discriminating test was confounded -- see cost.contention_sensitivity.
results.working_account: A per-message CPU-side cost in the device path -- plausibly a fence or flush making GPU writes visible to the NIC -- explains the small-message penalty and the crossover. The residual steady-state 5.5% is not explained by amortisation alone; coherence on host DMA is the leading candidate.
results.practical: Bandwidth turns positive at 16 KB, latency not until 256 KB -- a streaming benchmark keeps messages in flight and amortises the fixed cost, a ping-pong pays it every round trip. Production GPU HPC and LLM training move megabytes and sit far above both crossovers. The small-message penalty applies to halo exchanges and small collectives.

results.margin: The result INVERTS the idle-state gap, which is backwards for memory contention -- device transfers never touch the loaded DDR4.
results.confound: The load generator consumes cores as well as bandwidth. The GPU-direct path needs more host CPU, so core starvation swamped the effect under test. Recorded as confounded rather than reported as a number.

unplanned_finding.statement: GPU-direct is markedly more sensitive to CPU contention than host transfers -- 75% degradation versus 50%.
unplanned_finding.note: Nobody set out to measure this. It matters, because a real application is using its cores. It survives the confound because the confound IS the finding here.

results.next_step: Separate core pressure from bandwidth pressure -- pin the load generator off the ranks under test, or drive memory load from a different domain.

declared.source: hwloc device locality (captured); Slurm CoreSpecCount, /proc/cmdline, /proc/irq/*/smp_affinity_list, system.slice cpuset (NOT yet captured)

device_locality.note: Answered offline from declared/frontier-compute.hwloc.xml -- no machine time required.
device_locality.slingshot_nics: hsn0->NUMA3, hsn1->NUMA1, hsn2->NUMA0, hsn3->NUMA2 -- exactly one per domain, symmetric
device_locality.asymmetry: ens2 (management ethernet), nvme0n1, nvme1n1 and dma0chan0 ALL sit on NUMA 0
device_locality.implication: NUMA 0 carries three devices no other domain has. More interrupt handling and more DMA through one domain's memory controller. A job that is I/O heavy drives that traffic through NUMA 0 specifically.

not_yet_captured: Slurm CoreSpecCount / CpuSpecList -- would be a SECOND declared source for the 8 reserved cores, which currently rests on hwloc alone
system.slice cpuset -- where system services may run

results.next_step: srun -n1 -c 56 ./scripts/15_system_interference.sh on a compute node. Captures the four uncaptured declared sources, then measures a /proc/interrupts delta (where IRQs actually land vs where smp_affinity_list says) and per-core jitter (whether the reservation is sufficient at all). bin/jitter validated on corsys4: uniform jitter, no core above 2x the median -- correct for a box with no core specialization.
results.note: The device-locality asymmetry does NOT explain the uniform node-0 preference in the GPU host matrix: more devices predicts a SLOWER domain, and node 0 measured fastest. The probe-thread hypothesis stands.

flagged.statement: Per-GCD HBM latency spans 365-397 ns, and pairs (0,3), (1,4), (2,5) match within 0.3 ns.
flagged.why_flagged: That LOOKS like structure and sits inside the 37.6 ns noise band. Explicitly not claimed.

pitfalls.symptom: Latency measurements come out high with no error anywhere.
pitfalls.cause: THP is [never] and the hugetlb pool is empty (Total 4, Free 0). Both normal paths fail silently.
pitfalls.remedy: Load craype-hugepages2M -- it works by relinking, not a runtime flag. Then verify via smaps; do not trust the madvise return.
pitfalls.sting: Once linked, the default allocator ABORTS under a remote `numactl -m`, because the module provisions only the local node's pool. Local latency and the NUMA matrix need two separate passes.
pitfalls.provenance_note: THP setting and hugetlb pool are readable by anyone (/sys/kernel/mm/..., /proc/meminfo), and craype-hugepages2M is in the OLCF user guide. The '~16 ns high' figure was ours and is removed.

pitfalls.cause: One core per L3 group is OS-reserved: 0, 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, 56.
pitfalls.remedy: `-c 56` is the ceiling. It also divides cleanly: 14 cores / 28 threads per NUMA domain.
pitfalls.provenance_note: OLCF documents low-noise-mode core specialization; Cpus_allowed_list shows it to any process.

pitfalls.symptom: Topology conclusions drawn on a login node do not hold on compute.
pitfalls.cause: login08 is EPYC 7763 + a single MI210; compute is 7A53 + 4x MI250X.
pitfalls.remedy: Both are gfx90a so builds carry over, but no topology measurement from a login node is valid. Run 00_topo.sh inside an allocation.
pitfalls.provenance_note: Login and compute node specs are both published.

pitfalls.symptom: Inter-node bandwidth from one rank per node reads far below the node spec.
pitfalls.cause: One rank per node crosses one of four Slingshot NICs.
pitfalls.remedy: Spread ranks across the four NUMA domains -- `-c 14` gives one rank per domain.
pitfalls.provenance_note: Four NICs and the 100 GB/s figure are published. The 22.7/45.1/90.3 scaling was measured by us today and is removed from the declared rendering.

pitfalls.symptom: OSU 7.4 fails to build against the Cray toolchain.
pitfalls.cause: c/upc is unconditionally in the top-level SUBDIRS and there is no configure flag to disable it; the Cray compiler has no UPC front end.
pitfalls.provenance_note: We hit this building OSU. Not in any OLCF document.

pitfalls.symptom: The shipped Frontier build script fails or takes 4-8 hours.
pitfalls.cause: config/build_olcf_frontier_ROCm.sh hardcodes BOOST_ROOT to /ccs/proj/mat151 (inaccessible outside that project) and builds all eight variants.
pitfalls.remedy: Use the boost/1.86.0 module and build only gpu_real -- about 15 minutes.
pitfalls.provenance_note: We hit this building QMCPACK. Not in any OLCF document.

open_questions: Do the NUMA tiers hold across nodes? Single-node result; needs 8-16 short jobs.

Can measured distances be injected back via hwloc_distances_add, so existing consumers (MPI, Slurm, mpibind, ZeroSum) pick up corrected values with no code change? Unverified against the hwloc version on Frontier -- and if it works it is the strongest deployment path in the project.
Is the SLIT-vs-measured discrepancy already known to OLCF, or a known firmware simplification?
Read/write mix for loaded latency -- currently read-only.
Does the uniform node-0 host preference follow the probe's main thread? Re-run pinned to a different domain. If it does, it is our artifact; if not, it is a machine property with no declared source.
Does gpu.numa_affinity become measurable with more passes or a different probe? The effect, if any, is below 8% GPU-latency variance.
Does die parity hold across nodes? Currently one node.

observations.statement: Host-memory latency splits by GCD die parity. Even dies (0,2,4,6) mean 1382 ns; odd dies (1,3,5,7) mean 1224 ns. The slowest odd die beats the fastest even one in every pass.

conditions.host_memory: explicitly bound per NUMA domain, verified with move_pages

observations.why_promoted: July flagged this and declined to claim it for one specific reason: host memory used default hipHostMalloc placement, so the NUMA domain was uncontrolled and the absolute numbers were 'to some host domain'. That caveat is gone -- every allocation is now bound and verified. And the separation holds in all three passes tested INDEPENDENTLY, which pooling would not have established: pooling lets one lucky pass carry a result.
observations.secondary_structure: Even dies are also NUMA-sensitive (across-domain range 88-175 ns) while odd dies are nearly flat (27-55 ns), and even dies are far noisier pass-to-pass (129-155 ns vs 29-43 ns).
observations.consequence: Host-memory-bound kernels should prefer odd GCDs; peer-heavy kernels the even ones. Nothing in ROCm's placement logic knows this, and no declared source reports it.
observations.remaining_caveat: One node type, one node. Not established machine-wide.

hmat.finding: hwloc 2.11.2 defines six memory-attribute slots for cost on this machine and the firmware fills none of them. The container for measured cost exists, is typed, is per-(initiator, target), and is empty. Filling it is additive -- hwloc-annotate can register custom named attributes alongside these.
hmat.pointed_detail: The Read/Write split is finer than our own data. Our loaded-latency sweep is read-only and 'write traffic saturates differently' is an open question we recorded in July. hwloc has a named empty slot waiting for exactly that number.
